children: By Andy Serwer

Anthony Scaramucci just got his claim-to-fame record blasted, and he's laughing it off. You will, of course, recall that in July 2017 the Mooch served as President Donald Trump's press secretary for the briefest of brief tenures, which memed into a faux unit of measure. As in: One Scaramucci = 11 days.

Now, though, after Trump's latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, lasted only five days ending last Friday, Scaramucci's time in Washington looks like an eternity. The Zacharia imbroglio, not surprisingly, engenders some mixed-metaphor shtick from the Mooch. "She's like a thoroughbred," Scaramucci says. "This woman just blew right by me. She took my mantle. She kicked me out of The Guinness World Book of Records."

Kidding aside, Scaramucci says Zacharia should shut off social media and the news. "Washington can be a meat grinder and chop you up. It would be a mistake to take things personally, and I wouldn't want that to happen to her. I wish her well. I also believe that the universe did her a favor. Why, why, why, why do that job if you're not super-comfortable at the podium and being an extemporaneous speaker?"

By the way, does Scaramucci, 62 — who runs SkyBridge Capital, an investment firm, and SALT, an investor conference business, and does podcasts these days — mind being called "Mooch" (or is it "the Mooch")?

"I don't mind that, but I'll give you the history. I had a phys-ed teacher in the early 1970s out on Long Island, a German immigrant who had a visceral dislike of some of us. If you had a four-syllable last name, he picked one of the syllables of your last name. So, you know, if your name was Kryeski, you got called 'Kray,' and if your name was Scaramucci — he picked the third syllable of the four-syllable last name of mine and called me 'Mooch.'"

Truth be told, some people find the Mooch to be a little over the top, a bit full of bunkum. "Well, I mean, I am a little full of it," he says. "I'm somebody who's pretty authentic, though. I'm not going to BS people. I'm a salesperson by training. I'm a communicator. Some people will like what I'm saying, and some people will dislike it. I guess what I would say to people is, 'Get to know me.' I think if you get to know me, you'll realize that I'm probably not exactly who you think I am. There's probably a disconnect between what people think of me and who I actually am."
With the midterm elections less than two weeks away, I was curious what Scaramucci thought about the prospects for both the GOP and the Democrats.

"I think it will be good for the Democrats on the House side," he says. "David Axelrod, who's a little bit smarter than me, would say, 'Don't just look at the top line, look at the 435 districts.' I think the Democrats could pick up as many as 15 House seats and will win the House."

Mooch sees a toss-up in the upper house. "The Democrats should win the Senate," he says. "All the metrics don't look good for the Republicans. They look really bad for the President's approval rating on the economy. This is the only referendum that we have on a president, a two-year report card, which is basically a customer complaint desk on the presidency. And so the Democrats should resoundingly win the Senate, but it doesn't look that way to me. Maybe there ends up a tie, and Vance would be the deciding vote."
What would Scaramucci say to Trump if he were in his old role as White House press secretary?

"You got probably $700 or $800 million, Mr. President, of money that you raised in this MAGA PAC," Scaramucci says as if speaking directly to Trump. "Unleash the whole thing. You told a little bit of a fib this morning that you were going to put out $400 million. You and I both know you very well you're not going to do that. But that is what you really need to do. You're claiming that you're going to do 18 rallies between now and Election Day. I would probably dial that down to zero. Stop talking about the masculine parts of different candidates. I think it's coming across a little weird. Maybe you're getting some laugh lines out of that, but I don't think it's working for you."

Skipping ahead to the presidential election of 2028, Scaramucci thinks it will be Gavin Newsom on the Democratic side. "First, I always get this wrong," he caveats. Mooch also notes that he's a Republican. "So I know the Republicans — the Republicans go after the person that they know as their main adversary, and right now that is Newsom. He's a great debater, and he's got the name recognition" and the experience running the giant economy of California.
As for the GOP, Scaramucci sees Vice President JD Vance in the pole position, "even though the President's making him squirm and wouldn't necessarily endorse him or say positive things about him.

"To be the president, the No. 1 thing you need is name recognition. The second thing you need is money. You got to get a lot of money together, and you got to start that process. And Vance has already started that."
Scaramucci turned against Trump in August 2019 and has been a critic ever since. Whatever he thinks of Trump, doesn't the President deserve some credit for keeping the stock market up?

"The stock market is doing well," Scaramucci says. "I think it could be doing a lot better with a 3.96% 10-year Treasury yield as opposed to a plus-five or over 10-year, which Trump caused, frankly. I would make the case to you that the rich are getting richer, and while I love that, and I'm a stock market participant, there's a lot of our fellow Americans who aren't doing well. I think it's situational that the market's up. It's an induction of capital spending in AI, power centers, energy, et cetera, and not necessarily related to the President."

Are we in an artificial-intelligence bubble? "Ken Griffin's smarter than me, and he says we're in a bubble," Scaramucci says. "I'm not so sure. I feel like the spending wave is a tsunami still, even at higher interest rates. There are companies like Meta that are considering issuing new shares, which will be slightly dilutive, to make up for all of this massive spending. The economy is running hot as a result of all of this massive spending. Even Larry Fink [CEO of BlackRock] said, 'Man, if we stop or pause these data centers, we will probably slip into a recession.' Of course, we won't know if it's a bubble until after it bursts. But I wouldn't be betting against the current trend given what I know about capital flows right now."
After Scaramucci became disillusioned with Trump, he has been predicting Trump's downfall, but that hasn't happened. Why?

"He is a very successful politician," Mooch says. "Whether you like Donald Trump or dislike Donald Trump, we're 26 years into the 21st century and he is the looming figure of our time. He'll be on the stage because of this interregnum period for 12 years. He's altered America's brand internationally. He's also affected the way we see ourselves. And if you look at the polling numbers, 70-plus percent of the people feel that the country isn't going in the right direction. Eighty-plus percent of the people feel that the government's corrupt. But he's got two years left to go. Let's say he loses both houses, he'll be somewhat neutered, but he'll be more bombastic, more potentially dangerous."
Pontificating thusly is part of Scaramucci's day job now. He hosts a popular podcast, The Rest Is Politics: US, with British journalist Katty Kay, which is apparently a smash hit in Britain.

His other job is on Wall Street. Scaramucci founded asset manager SkyBridge in 2005 after co-founding investment partnership Oscar Capital Management (which was sold to Neuberger Berman in 2001), and before that he had a stint at Goldman Sachs.

SkyBridge now has some $2 billion in AUM, down several billion from its peak. At one point, the firm throttled investor redemptions and reduced staff. Scaramucci says the business is in good shape now and refocused with some 60% in crypto, an investment class in which Scaramucci is a true believer.

Speaking of crypto and SkyBridge, in 2022, Mooch sold 30% of his firm to Sam Bankman-Fried. Did he get the money back? "I'm not allowed to talk about that because of the litigation involved," he says.
Will Trump pardon SBF?

"Well, that I am allowed to talk about," he says. "Sam hurt me in a lot of different ways. I trusted Sam and he hurt my reputation. He hurt many, many people with what he did. [But] I feel like a 25-year sentence for a young man like that is probably too much. If he had pled out, he would have probably had a lower sentence. A lot of his fellow employees are already out of jail, and a lot of people got their money back through the bankruptcy process, but I don't think the President will pardon him because I think that sort of would have happened already."

As for Mooch running for office, don't count on it. "Nassau County dogcatcher might be available," he says. Still, the political bug hasn't completely left him. "Would I work in a capacity somewhere in somebody's presidential campaign again? The answer to that is yes," he says. "Not as an elected official, but I would work with somebody to help them raise money or potentially some communications."

And stay with the candidate if they win the White House? "I would never rule anything out. I have told a few presidential candidates I want just one more day in the White House, which would make it an even dozen for me."
